title: First Law of Thermodynamics
topicTitle: Meaning of thermal equilibrium and Zeroth law of thermodynamics
notes: The first law is energy conservation for a thermodynamic system. With heat Q positive into the system and work W positive when done by the system, ΔU=Q−W. Internal energy U is a state function; heat and work are energy transfers across the boundary.
For a gas expanding against constant pressure, W=PΔV. If 500 J of heat enters and the gas does 180 J of work, then ΔU=500−180=320 J.
At constant volume, boundary work is zero, so Q=ΔU if no other work is present. In an adiabatic process Q=0 and ΔU=−W. Over a full cycle ΔU=0, hence net Q=net W.
For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU=(3/2)nRΔT. For 2 mol heated by 10 K, ΔU≈(3/2)(2)(8.314)(10)=249 J, independent of the path between the states.
A p–V diagram makes work visible: work done by a gas is the area under the process curve, W=∫P dV. Expansion gives positive work under this convention; compression gives negative work.
confusion: Some books define work on the system as positive and write ΔU=Q+Won; do not mix conventions.
At constant volume, Q=ΔU only if no other work is present.

specificConditions: **Energy Conservation Foundation:** The first law ($\Delta U = Q - W$) is energy conservation applied to thermodynamic systems. Internal energy $U$ is a state function; heat $Q$ and work $W$ are path-dependent energy transfers. The sign convention: $Q > 0$ when heat enters the system, $W > 0$ when work is done BY the system.

**Process Dependence:** $Q$ and $W$ depend on the thermodynamic path (isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric, isochoric), but $\Delta U$ depends only on initial and final states. For a cyclic process, $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q = W$ — net heat in equals net work out.

**Work in Thermodynamics:** Only $PV$-work is considered in the basic first law: $W = \int P_{ext} dV$. Reversible work uses the system pressure $W = \int P dV$. Other work forms (electrical, surface tension, magnetic) must be added as extra terms if present.
